name: Fort Cass
notes: Principal Cherokee Agency; General Winfield Scott's headquarters; primary emigration depot for Cherokee-managed detachments.

name: Ross's Landing
notes: Major departure point for the water route removals. Now the site of downtown Chattanooga.

name: Fort Butler
notes: North Carolina removal headquarters. Held up to 1,500 Cherokee during the roundup.

name: Fort Payne
notes: Departure point for the John Benge detachment (southern route). The city of Fort Payne, AL is named after this fort.

name: Fort Marr
notes: The only surviving original stockade structure from the Cherokee removal period.

name: Fort Lindsay
notes: Northeastern-most military installation for the removal. Located near the junction of the Nantahala and Little Tennessee Rivers.

name: Fort Montgomery
notes: Removal fort in Graham County, NC.

name: Fort Hembree
notes: Removal fort in Clay County, NC.

name: Fort Delaney
notes: Convergence point for North Carolina removal routes.

name: New Echota / Fort Wool
notes: Military fort built in the Cherokee national capital. General Scott initially arrived here on May 17, 1838. Now a Georgia state historic site.

name: Gunter's Landing
notes: Major emigration depot, named after Cherokee leader John Gunter.

name: Red Clay Council Ground
notes: Cherokee national capital after 1832, when Georgia outlawed Cherokee government meetings at New Echota. Known as "Camp Ross" during the removal. Now Red Clay State Historic Park.

name: Rattlesnake Springs
notes: Assembly site where the last Cherokee council on eastern soil was held on August 1, 1838.
